Careah
kah-REE-ah
n. (the father of Johanan, a captain of the remnant after the fall of Jerusalem; spelled Kareah in Jeremiah)
Hebrew Qareach, bald, from qarach, to make bald; the Authorized Version spells the name Careah at 2 Kings 25:23 and Kareah in Jeremiah.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Careah is named as the father of Johanan, the captain who warned Gedaliah of the plot against his life: “And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, there came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Careah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men” (2 Kings 25:23). Jeremiah spells the same name Kareah: “Then they came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah” (Jeremiah 40:8). One man, two spellings in the same English Bible. The name means bald. Gedaliah's charge to these captains was to accept the settlement Babylon offered: “And Gedaliah sware to them, and to their men, and said unto them, Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you” (2 Kings 25:24). It was good counsel and it was Jeremiah's counsel too. After the murder, fear overruled it: “And all the people, both small and great, and the captains of the armies, arose, and came to Egypt: for they were afraid of the Chaldees” (2 Kings 25:26).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Careah is a biblical proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.

expand to see more

Careah is the name of the father of Johanan the captain; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

It occurs once in this spelling, at 2 Kings 25:23.

Jeremiah spells the same name Kareah, as at Jeremiah 40:8.

The Hebrew means bald, from qarach, to make bald.

His son Johanan warned Gedaliah of Ishmael's plot.

Key Scripture

2Ki 25:23 — "And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, there came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Careah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men."

Jer 40:8 — "Then they came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, and the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, and Jezaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men."

2Ki 25:24 — "And Gedaliah sware to them, and to their men, and said unto them, Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you."

2Ki 25:26 — "And all the people, both small and great, and the captains of the armies, arose, and came to Egypt: for they were afraid of the Chaldees."

Modern Corruption

Fear is treated as a sufficient reason for disobedience, where the remnant went down into Egypt against the plain word of God because they were afraid.

expand to see more

The last act of the kingdom of Judah is a flight to Egypt, and the text gives the motive without dressing it up: they were afraid of the Chaldees. Jeremiah had told them plainly to stay, and they went anyway, carrying the prophet with them. Fear is a real thing and Scripture never mocks it; but fear is not an argument, and a believer who makes it one will find himself in Egypt.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Gedaliah's counsel to dwell in the land was God's counsel, and that one murder was enough to overthrow it in the minds of men who had already decided they were safer elsewhere.
